newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler turns to GM's Delphi for fuel cell engine.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler turns to GM's Delphi for fuel cell engine.

text.p: Chrysler Corp. said Tuesday it has turned to the components division of one of its archrivals, General Motors Corp., to develop a 40 horsepower engine for its experimental fuel cell vehicle.

Delphi Energy and Engine Management Systems, a unit of GM's Delphi Automotive Systems, signed a multi-million dollar contract to develop the costly and complicated fuel cell. The engine extracts hydrogen from gasoline, then uses the hydrogen to create electricity to power the vehicle.
Chrysler and Delphi made the announcement at the SAE International Congress & Exposition, an annual gathering of auto industry suppliers and automakers in Detroit.

Chrysler unveiled its plans to develop an on-board fuel cell prototype vehicle in January at the North American International Auto Show in Detroit. The Delphi contract was signed Dec. 13, 1996, but an announcement was postponed until the SAE conference.
Officials from both companies would not disclose how much they are spending on the project, which is being built without federal money.

"For some, the temptation may be to think of Delphi as part of GM -- one of our competitors, or as simply a major automotive supplier," said Bernard Robertson, vice president of engineering technologies and general manager of Chrysler's Jeep/Truck operations.
"But on this program, Delphi is a partner -- a company which shares our vision for the viability of a gasoline-powered fuel-cell vehicle," he said.
The two companies already have a close relationship. Delphi is Chrysler's eighth largest supplier. Chrysler ranks as the second or third largest customer for Delphi behind GM, which is the largest.
With the announcement, Delphi becomes Chrysler's major partner in the fuel cell venture.

Delphi played a major role in developing the engine for GM's EV1 electric vehicle. While Delphi works on the engine components, Chrysler will develop an electric drivetrain, control strategy and work on integrating the multitude of other systems into the total vehicle.

Donald Runkle, general manager of Delphi Energy & Management, said the company will subcontract out some smaller parts of the fuel cell technology. He said high costs remain a major hurdle for the engine.

Because it is based on gasoline, Chrysler believes its fuel cell concept advances the technology forward by 10 years. Previous development attempts have been held back by difficulties in supplying and storing hydrogen.

Chrysler hopes to have its "proof of concept" vehicle built within two years. Fuel cell power sources have good future potential, the company believes, because they are 50 percent more efficient and 90 percent cleaner than conventionl gasoline engines; have a range of up to 400 miles; and would cost no more than today's mid-sized cars.
